observations: A bird-like figure stands upright on thin legs at center; its body is built from dense overlapping strokes in deep red, dark blue, and near-black, with scattered white flecks throughout the plumage.
A flat, solid yellow beak juts left from a round head; a single grey eye sits above it, and a blue-grey cast shadow falls behind the figure against the flat cobalt background.
The tail and crest fan outward in loose, radiating strokes of red, purple, white, and blue, contrasting with the compact white oval of the chest, which is the only large unstroked area in the image.
reading: The figure holds its ground with a sideways glance that reads as wary rather than aggressive. Dense layered strokes build the body into something heavy and ruffled, while the plain yellow beak and white chest patch cut through the darkness with blunt simplicity. The flat blue field keeps everything still, and the shadow anchors the figure to a surface, giving the restless mark-making an unexpected calm.
contextAngle: Within the owned nnotb subset, this work sits between title neighbors nnxyz nnotb #55 and nnxyz nnotb #57. All three use a single flat background color, but #56 is the only one of the three where the figure and background share a cool blue tone rather than contrasting sharply.

connections.reason: Both works place a densely stroked figure against the same flat cobalt blue field, making the background color a shared formal anchor despite the very different subjects.

Where #56 uses radiating strokes to suggest softness and wariness, title neighbor #57 uses the same radiating line energy to build a wide-open mouth and bulging eyes, showing the same stroke pattern carrying opposite emotional weight.

lookingQuestion: The white chest patch is the only large area left free of overlapping strokes — what does its placement between the dense body and the thin legs do to how you read the figure's weight?
ambiguities: The title 'nnotb #56' is treated as content only; no subject identification is drawn from it.
Title-derived order and recorded-creation order align for this work in the owned subset, but gaps elsewhere in the family mean neither confirms a strict making sequence.
